outcome: No classification of graphs with representation number 3 has appeared since 26 January 2024, and the Wikipedia article (footer: last edited 9 August 2026) still says none is known; the window holds classifications restricted to split graphs, split comparability graphs, well-partitioned chordal graphs, co-bipartite graphs and melon graphs, family results (grid graphs, cylindric grid graphs, bounds for circulants), and one bipartite upper bound (crown graphs extremal, preprint of 24 September 2026) whose authors credit ChatGPT models with its approach; none of these settles the general question.
problem_asks: (a) A classification (characterization, forbidden-subgraph description, or explicit list) of the class of all graphs G with representation number R(G) = 3, where R(G) is the least k such that G has a word in which each letter occurs exactly k times and two letters alternate exactly when their vertices are adjacent. (b) Equivalently, since R(G) = 3 means G is 3-representable and not 2-representable: which 3-representable graphs fail to be circle graphs (2-representable graphs are the non-complete circle graphs, and complete graphs have R = 1). (c) The statement places no restriction on the graphs (no bipartite, split, co-bipartite or other family), so a complete answer must cover every graph; a classification that holds only inside a subclass answers part of (a) and leaves the rest.

events.what_happened: Sergey Kitaev, 'On graphs with representation number 3' (arXiv 1403.1616, 6 March 2014; the journal version appeared in the Journal of Automata, Languages and Combinatorics in 2015, per a search listing I did not open). Before this paper the only known members of the class were the Petersen graph and the triangular prism. It shows that every prism belongs to the class (Theorem 18: for n >= 4, the prism Pr_n is not 2-word-representable, so R(Pr_n) = 3), that two extension operations preserve membership (Theorem 19: the class contains the Petersen graph, the prisms, and every graph obtained from these by operations 1 and 2 applied any number of times in any order), and that the class is not contained in any c-colourable class (Theorem 24). Section 8 poses Problems 2 and 3 (on k-comparability graphs and crown graphs H_{k,k} lying in R_{k-l}); neither asks for the classification of R_3. Section 6 poses Problem 1: can each bipartite graph be 3-word-represented?
events.revisions: v1 6 Mar 2014 is the only version listed on the arXiv abstract page; journal version 2015 per a search listing (not opened).
events.delivers: Membership in R_3 for all prisms and for every graph obtained from the Petersen graph and prisms by the two operations; each such graph has R exactly 3 (the prisms are not 2-representable). Shows R_3 has no bounded chromatic number. Restricted to these families; no statement about which other graphs lie in R_3.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks: no membership test for arbitrary graphs, and no description of R_3 beyond the families named. Problem 1 of Section 6 (3-representability of bipartite graphs) was answered negatively by Glen, Kitaev and Pyatkin (2016, event glen-kitaev-pyatkin-2016-crowns); I did not confirm that this is the same question as Kitaev-Lozin Problem 7.2.7, which the 2016 abstract cites.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2015 (per search listing; the journal page was not opened)

events.directly_checkable: The prism result is checkable by hand from the circle-graph criterion: the prism Pr_n for n >= 4 is not a circle graph. I did not re-derive the paper's proof.
events.direction: Enlarges the known R_3: adds infinite families (prisms and their extensions) and shows R_3 is not inside any fixed c-colourable class. It says nothing about whether a finite list of forbidden subgraphs or any other description exists.
events.object: The prism graphs Pr_n for n >= 4 are the exhibited members with R = 3, shown by an explicit non-2-representability argument (Theorem 18). The two extension operations are explicit constructions; no counterexample to any claim is involved.

events.what_happened: Ozgur Akgun, Ian P. Gent, Sergey Kitaev and Hans Zantema, 'Solving computational problems in the theory of word-representable graphs' (arXiv 1808.01215, 3 August 2018; Journal of Integer Sequences 22 (2019), Article 19.2.5, per a search listing). Using semi-transitive orientations they enumerate connected non-word-representable graphs up to 11 vertices, which corrected a published result, and they report the distribution of k-representable graphs on at most 9 vertices, finding a new 9-vertex graph with high representation number. The abstract I opened gives no count for representation number 3. Search snippets (not verified against the paper) report that the only 6-vertex graph with R = 3 is the triangular prism and that 39 graphs on 7 vertices have R = 3.
events.revisions: v1 3 Aug 2018 is the only version I saw; journal version 2019 per search listing.
events.delivers: Computational census data on representation numbers for graphs of at most 9 vertices (and a full enumeration of non-word-representable graphs to 11 vertices). It is data, not a theorem about R = 3: it gives no description of the class at any order I could read, and holds only for small orders.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks; a census to 9 vertices covers no infinite family.

Separately, Kitaev and Sun (arXiv 2110.05405, not opened) report two misclassified 7-vertex graphs in earlier published enumerations; this bears on census reliability at small orders, not on any specific R = 3 claim.
events.direction: No direction for R = 3: census data at orders up to 9 (and non-word-representable graphs up to 11).

ai.disclosed_cost: Abstract states that the enumeration took 3 CPU years of computation.

events.what_happened: Marc Glen, Sergey Kitaev and Artem Pyatkin, 'On the representation number of a crown graph' (arXiv 1609.00674, 2 September 2016; Discrete Applied Mathematics 244 (2018), pp. 89-93, per a search listing). For n >= 5 the crown graph H_{n,n} (K_{n,n} minus a perfect matching) has representation number ceil(n/2). Per its abstract, it completely solves Kitaev-Lozin Problem 7.4.2 and gives a negative answer to Problem 7.2.7 of Kitaev-Lozin on 3-word-representability of bipartite graphs.
events.revisions: v1 2 Sep 2016 is the only version I saw; journal version DAM 2018 per search listing.
events.delivers: For crown graphs only: R(H_{n,n}) = ceil(n/2) for n >= 5. So H_{5,5} and H_{6,6} have R = 3, while H_{n,n} for n >= 7 has R >= 4; hence not every bipartite graph is 3-representable. Says nothing about graphs outside the crown family.
events.remains: Classification of R = 3 for every other class and for general graphs.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2018, per search listing; the journal page was not opened)

events.directly_checkable: The crown graphs H_{n,n} are explicit; the lower bounds are combinatorial arguments the paper proves. I did not re-derive them.
events.direction: Cuts against the expectation that bipartite graphs are 3-representable: crown graphs with n >= 7 have R >= 4. Not a classification of R = 3.
events.object: The crown graphs H_{n,n}, n >= 5, with exact representation numbers ceil(n/2) by proof (the paper establishes both bounds).

events.what_happened: Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna, 'Words for the Graphs with Permutation-Representation Number at most Three' (arXiv 2307.00301, 1 July 2023). The abstract states that a characterization of graphs with permutation-representation number at most three is open, and that the paper determines the permutation-representation number and the representation number of book graphs. I did not find the NP-completeness statement in the abstract page; a search summary attributes it to this paper.
events.revisions: v1 1 Jul 2023 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: Representation number of book graphs (values not read in the abstract). Concerns prn for the classes it studies; the R = 3 question is touched only for book graphs.
events.remains: Classification of R = 3 for all graphs; the prn <= 3 characterization is stated as open by the authors.
events.direction: Partial results on book graphs; no classification.

events.what_happened: Tithi Dwary and K. V. Krishna, 'Word-representability of graphs with respect to split recomposition' (arXiv 2401.01954, v1 3 January 2024). They show word-representable graphs are closed under split recomposition, determine the representation number of the recomposed graph in terms of its parts, and deduce that parity graphs are word-representable.
events.revisions: v1 3 Jan 2024 is the only version listed.
events.delivers: A formula for R of a split recomposition of word-representable graphs (formula not read). Not a classification of R = 3 graphs.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Reduction result: R of recomposed graphs from the parts. Not about the R = 3 class directly.

events.what_happened: Zion Hefty, Paul Horn, Colby Muir and Andrew Owens, 'Word-Representable Graphs: Orientations, Posets, and Bounds', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 31(4) (2024), #P4.2, DOI 10.37236/12806. The journal abstract (opened) says the authors introduce tools from partially ordered sets, Ramsey theory and probabilistic methods and 'settle a number of open problems in the field, regarding both the existence and length of word-representations for various classes of graphs'. The abstract does not mention representation number. A search summary of the paper (not verified) reports a Ramsey-based construction of graphs of arbitrarily high girth that are not word-representable, and says little is known about what forces representation number to be large. The submission date (16 February 2024) and acceptance/publication dates come from the NSF PAR record as reported by a search result; I did not open that record (its PDF returned binary), and I did not locate an arXiv posting.
events.revisions: Journal publication 4 Oct 2024 (per search summary). A later version adds finite geometry to the tools list (per search summary; not verified). No arXiv identifier located.
events.delivers: Not established for R = 3: the abstract concerns existence and length of word-representations for various classes, and the search summary suggests bounds on large representation numbers. Neither is shown to touch graphs with R = 3.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, as far as the abstract shows.

events.what_happened: Biswajit Das and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian, 'Square-free word-representation of word-representable graphs' (arXiv 2402.14426, v1 22 February 2024). Every non-empty word-representable graph has a square-free representation; for a word-representable G with R(G) = k, every k-uniform representing word is square-free; infinitely many square-free words represent a connected non-complete word-representable graph.
events.revisions: v1 22 Feb 2024 is the only version listed.
events.delivers: A property of k-uniform representing words (square-freeness). It identifies no graph with R = 3 and classifies none. Discarded as off-question: a square-freeness result, not a result on which graphs have R = 3.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Not about the R = 3 class.

events.what_happened: Tithi Dwary and K. V. Krishna, 'Characterization of word-representable graphs using modular decomposition' (arXiv 2412.17648, v1 23 December 2024; published in Communications in Combinatorics and Optimization in September 2025, per a search listing, not opened). They characterize word-representable graphs via modular decomposition and give the representation number of a word-representable decomposable graph G with modular partition P as R(G) = max{R(G/P), R^p(G[M_1]), ..., R^p(G[M_k])} (Theorem 2.7(2)), where R^p is the permutation-representation number. They also answer the Kitaev-Lozin question on lexicographic products. The paper states that Kitaev's earlier identity R(G_a[M]) = max{k, k'} with k' = R(M) is false, with Example 1: the wheel W6 has R = 3 although its module C6 has R = 2.
events.revisions: v1 23 Dec 2024 is the only arXiv version listed; journal version per search listing.
events.delivers: A reduction: the representation number of any word-representable graph is determined by its quotient graph and the permutation-representation numbers of its modules. This makes R = 3 for a modular graph a question about its quotient and modules, which are not themselves classified here.
events.remains: Classification of R = 3: the reduction still needs the quotient and module classes to be known, and no class of R = 3 graphs is described.
events.directly_checkable: The W6 example (K2 with one vertex replaced by C6) is a concrete graph whose R = 3 can be checked from the paper's example; I did not re-derive it.
events.direction: Reduction result that also corrects an earlier identity of Kitaev. Not a classification of R = 3 graphs.
events.object: Example 1 in the paper: the wheel W6, obtained by replacing a vertex of K2 with C6, given as a graph with R = 3 whose module C6 has R = 2. It is an example, not a counterexample to a conjecture about R = 3.

events.what_happened: Biswajit Das and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian, 'Word-representability of co-bipartite graph' (arXiv 2501.10112, v1 17 January 2025). Gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a co-bipartite graph to have a semi-transitive orientation, and states that characterizing word-representable co-bipartite graphs was open. The abstract does not mention representation number. An arXiv admin note records textual overlap with arXiv:1709.09725 by other authors.
events.revisions: v1 17 Jan 2025 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: A semi-transitive orientation criterion for co-bipartite graphs. It does not address representation number, so it bears on R = 3 only as the precursor of the 2025 co-bipartite representation-number result below.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: arXiv admin note: text overlaps with arXiv:1709.09725 (other authors). Not examined.
events.direction: Not about R = 3 directly.

events.what_happened: Tithi Dwary, Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna, 'Representation Number of Word-Representable Split Graphs' (arXiv 2502.00872; v1 2 February 2025, v2 27 April 2025). A split graph has a vertex set partitioned into a clique and an independent set. The authors show that every word-representable split graph has R <= 3, and they characterize the word-representable split graphs with R = 3 (v2 Theorem 3.2: G has R = 3 if and only if G contains an induced graph from the family C3 = F0, the even-k suns (k >= 4), and the odd-k graphs F1(k), F2(k) (k >= 5)). They also characterize split comparability graphs with R = 3 (Theorem 3.4: iff G contains F0 or F1(5) as an induced subgraph). The v2 comment says Fig. 2 was corrected using N. Pardal's PhD thesis, and the proof of Theorem 6 and the subsequent split-comparability results were updated. The family definitions were relayed by a summarising fetch and not read in full.
events.revisions: v1 2 Feb 2025; v2 27 Apr 2025 (Fig. 2 corrected from N. Pardal's thesis; proof of Theorem 6 and split-comparability results updated).
events.delivers: Within the class of word-representable split graphs: R <= 3 always, and R = 3 exactly for graphs containing one of the listed induced families (Theorem 3.2 as relayed by the fetch). Within split comparability graphs: R = 3 exactly when F0 or F1(5) is induced (Theorem 3.4). A characterization of R = 3 restricted to split graphs; it says nothing about graphs that are not split.
events.remains: R = 3 for all word-representable graphs that are not split (in particular all non-split comparability and non-comparability graphs). The authors' conclusion asks next to characterize word-representable split graphs by minimal forbidden induced subgraphs.

checked_by.qualification: Author of a PhD thesis that the v2 comment cites for corrected figures; thesis not located
checked_by.what_they_did: Thesis cited as the source for the corrections to Fig. 2 in v2 (not independently checked)

events.directly_checkable: The forbidden induced families can be checked by hand on any given split graph; I did not check the families in full.
events.doubts: The authors changed the statement's supporting material between v1 and v2: Fig. 2 graphs were corrected and the proof of Theorem 6 was revised, with knock-on changes to the split-comparability results. What exactly changed in the stated characterization was not compared across versions here.
events.direction: Gives an exact characterization of R = 3 within split graphs and split comparability graphs. It cuts in the direction the bullet expects for those subclasses (R = 3 is determined by explicit forbidden induced families). It is not a classification of R = 3 in general.

events.what_happened: Tithi Dwary, Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna, 'Characterization of Split Comparability Graphs' (arXiv 2504.19167, v1 27 April 2025). They characterize split comparability graphs by vertex labelling and show that their permutation-representation number is at most three, and they determine those with prn exactly three. The abstract concerns prn only and does not mention R.
events.revisions: v1 27 Apr 2025 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: Results on the permutation-representation number of split comparability graphs. Not representation number. Discarded for this bullet, but recorded because the same authors' split-comparability characterization of R = 3 sits alongside it.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Not about R = 3.

events.what_happened: Tithi Dwary and K. V. Krishna, 'Word-representability of well-partitioned chordal graphs' (arXiv 2504.04256, v1 5 April 2025; author names from a search listing). Using split decomposition, they show that the representation number of a word-representable well-partitioned chordal graph is at most three, and they determine the class of such graphs with representation number exactly three. They also give polynomial recognition and a minimal forbidden induced subgraph characterization of circle graphs within the class. The abstract (opened) states these results; the theorem statements were not read.
events.revisions: v1 5 Apr 2025 is the only version listed.
events.delivers: Within well-partitioned chordal graphs: R <= 3 always, and the R = 3 subclass is determined (the characterization was not read). Restricted to that class; no statement about graphs outside it.
events.remains: R = 3 for all graphs outside well-partitioned chordal graphs.
events.direction: Partial classification of R = 3 inside a restricted class, in the direction R = 3 is the top value (R <= 3).

events.what_happened: Biswajit Das and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian, 'p-complete square-free word-representation of word-representable graphs' (arXiv 2505.05110; v1 8 May 2025, v2 24 December 2025). The abstract (opened) states that any 3-complete square-free uniform word-representable graph has representation number at most three; it gives complete characterizations of the p = 1 and p = 2 cases and a constructive method for p = 3.
events.delivers: R <= 3 for a subclass defined by a square-free and K_3-complete condition. It gives an upper bound, not a classification of R = 3, and the p = 3 case is constructive only.
events.remains: R = 3 classification for all graphs; the restricted class is not characterized for p = 3.
events.direction: Upper bound R <= 3 within a restricted class. Does not decide which graphs have R = 3.

events.what_happened: Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna, 'On the Conjecture of the Representation Number of Bipartite Graphs' (arXiv 2506.01057, 1 June 2025). Every bipartite graph with smaller partite set of size m has R <= 1 + ceil(m/2) (Corollary 1); for odd m with 5 <= m <= n, R <= ceil(m/2) (Theorem 3.1); and the Glen et al. conjecture R <= ceil((m+n)/4) is established for most bipartite graphs, with the case of equal even partite sizes left open (abstract), with partial results for subclasses (Theorems 4.1, 4.2). The paper gives no classification of bipartite graphs with R = 3.
events.revisions: v1 1 Jun 2025 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on R for bipartite graphs, and the Glen et al. bound for most bipartite graphs. Does not classify R = 3 graphs, bipartite or otherwise; it leaves open the equal-even-partite case.
events.remains: Classification of R = 3 for all graphs, and specifically which bipartite graphs have R = 3.
events.direction: Upper bounds on R for bipartite graphs. Does not decide any particular R = 3 membership.

events.what_happened: Nawaf Shafi Alshammari, Sergey Kitaev and Artem Pyatkin, 'On the representation number of grid graphs and cylindric grid graphs' (arXiv 2507.16469, 22 July 2025). Theorem 1: for m, n >= 3, R(Gr_{m,n}) = 3 for the grid graphs. Theorem 2: for m, n >= 3, R(CGr_{m,n}) = 3 for the cylindric grid graphs (the abstract states the cylindric hypothesis as m >= 2, which differs from the theorem). Conjecture 1: for toroidal grids with n, m >= 3 and m + n >= 8, R >= 4. The paper states the Petersen graph and prisms as known R = 3 graphs. Acknowledgements mention Sobolev Institute funding; no AI statement.
events.revisions: v1 22 Jul 2025 is the only version listed on the abstract page. A search snippet says the paper was accepted by the Journal of Automata, Languages and Combinatorics in February 2026; I did not verify this.
events.delivers: Adds two infinite families to the R = 3 class (grid graphs with m, n >= 3; cylindric grid graphs with m, n >= 3 per Theorem 2). Also conjectures a lower bound of 4 for toroidal grids. Restricted to these families; no classification.
events.remains: The R = 3 class outside grids and cylindric grids; and the toroidal conjecture is unresolved as far as I know.
events.directly_checkable: Grid graphs are explicit; the R = 3 claims are established by proof in the paper, which I did not re-derive.
events.doubts: The abstract's hypothesis for the cylindric case (m >= 2) differs from Theorem 2 (m, n >= 3). Only the stated theorem's hypothesis is recorded here.
events.direction: Enlarges the known R = 3 class by two families; the conjecture would extend the boundary to R >= 4. Not a classification.
events.object: The grid graphs Gr_{m,n} and cylindric grid graphs CGr_{m,n} (m, n >= 3) as families with representation number exactly 3, established by proof.

events.what_happened: Suchanda Roy and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian, 'On the word-representability of 5-regular circulant graphs' (arXiv 2512.05480, 5 December 2025). Theorem 3.13: for C_{2n}(2,1,n) with n > 3, the graph is word-representable and R <= 3. Other theorems (3.11, 3.12, 3.14, 3.15) give R <= 5 or R <= 5 + min{p,q} for factorizable cases. The paper gives no exact value of R = 3 for any circulant family. A footnote says a preliminary version was accepted for presentation at CALDAM 2026 (not verified).
events.revisions: v1 5 Dec 2025 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on R for 5-regular circulant graphs, including R <= 3 for one parametric family C_{2n}(2,1,n). No exact R = 3 identification.
events.remains: Exact representation numbers for the circulant families; the R = 3 class outside these families.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted a preliminary version for presentation (per footnote; not verified)

events.what_happened: Biswajit Das and Ramesh Hariharasubramanian, 'Word-representable co-bipartite graphs: vertex ordering, representation number, speed, and entropy' (arXiv 2509.03064; v1 3 September 2025, v2 2 June 2026). They give necessary and sufficient conditions, in terms of a vertex ordering, for a co-bipartite graph to be word-representable. Theorem 20: the representation number of every word-representable co-bipartite graph is at most 3. Corollary 22: if a word-representable co-bipartite graph is not a permutation graph, its representation number is 3. The abstract states that permutation graphs are the only co-bipartite graphs with representation number 2. The paper also gives speed 2^{O(n log n)} and entropy 0. The v2 page does not describe what changed.
events.revisions: v1 3 Sep 2025; v2 2 Jun 2026 (changes not described on the page).
events.delivers: Within the class of word-representable co-bipartite graphs: R = 2 exactly for permutation graphs, and R = 3 for every other word-representable co-bipartite graph (Theorem 20 and Corollary 22). Hence R = 3 is completely determined inside that class. Restricted to co-bipartite graphs; it says nothing about the other classes.
events.remains: R = 3 for all graphs outside co-bipartite graphs, which includes most of the class the bullet asks about.
events.directly_checkable: Permutation graphs and co-bipartite graphs are explicit; the ordering criterion can be checked on a given graph. I did not check the criterion on any example.
events.doubts: The v2 (June 2026) changes are not described on the abstract page, and the theorem proofs were not read. The fetch tool rendered some '3' symbols as '33' (formatting only).
events.direction: Complete determination of R = 3 within co-bipartite graphs: all word-representable non-permutation co-bipartite graphs have R = 3. Cuts in the direction the statement's partition would suggest for that subclass; it is not a classification of all R = 3 graphs.

events.what_happened: Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna, 'Word-Representation of Melon Graphs' (arXiv 2602.14179, v1 15 February 2026; to appear in Graphs and Combinatorics per the arXiv comment). Melon graphs are series-parallel graphs built from constituent paths. Theorem 2.2: every melon graph is 3-word-representable. Theorem 2.3: R(M) = 3 if and only if M contains an induced subgraph from M3 or M4 (M3: melon graphs with three constituent paths each of length at least three; M4: four constituent paths, one of length one and the others of length at least three). The prose in the paper's discussion reads 'three if and only if it has three constituent paths', which I read as consistent with Theorem 2.3 in effect (M4 contains three long paths) but did not confirm. Theorem 3.1 characterizes melon graphs that are comparability graphs; Theorem 3.5 gives prn = 3 conditions; Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 characterize word-representable line graphs of melon graphs and their representation number (per the HTML fetch, which summarised the theorems).
events.revisions: v1 15 Feb 2026 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: For melon graphs (a restricted class of series-parallel graphs): R <= 3 always, and R = 3 exactly on an induced-subgraph condition (Theorem 2.3). Restricted to melon graphs and, per the same paper, line graphs of melon graphs (R <= 3). It is a classification of R = 3 within melon graphs, not of graphs in general.
events.remains: R = 3 for all graphs outside melon graphs and their line graphs; the authors' conclusion asks for the representation number of series-parallel graphs in general.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal (acceptance inferred from 'to appear'; not verified)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication (per the arXiv comment; not verified)

events.directly_checkable: A melon graph is explicit from its constituent path lengths; the condition for R = 3 in Theorem 2.3 can be checked on a given melon graph. I did not check it on examples.
events.doubts: Internal wording: the prose 'three constituent paths' and Theorem 2.3's induced-subgraph condition are not identical as written, and Theorem 4.2 uses length at least two where the melon class uses length at least three. The fetch tool summarised the theorems and I could not read the PDF text to resolve these. A third-party AI-generated review (themoonlight.io; not opened, HTTP 429) summarises R = 2 when at most two long paths.
events.direction: Complete classification of R = 3 within melon graphs and (per Theorem 4.2) line graphs of melon graphs. Restricted; does not classify R = 3 in general.

events.what_happened: Matthew J. Colbrook and Catherine Drysdale, 'Crown graphs maximise the representation number of bipartite graphs' (arXiv 2609.35842, submitted 24 September 2026, v1 only seen). Theorem 1.1: every finite simple bipartite graph G on N >= 9 vertices has R(G) <= ceil(N/4). Combined with the known crown-graph value (Glen, Kitaev, Pyatkin 2016), crown graphs are extremal among bipartite graphs of the same order; the abstract says this settles the conjecture of Glen et al. The proof builds on a construction of Mozhui and Krishna (2025). The abstract says two finite assertions are each established by a checked Boolean unsatisfiability certificate, and that the main theorem and crown-extremality corollary have been formalised and verified in Lean 4. Section 6.2 contains the authors' AI declaration (see ai).
events.revisions: v1 24 Sep 2026 is the only version I saw.
events.delivers: An upper bound R(G) <= ceil(N/4) for every bipartite graph on N >= 9 vertices, with crown graphs extremal. Consequences for R = 3 within bipartite graphs: every bipartite graph on at least 9 and at most 12 vertices has R <= 3, so a bipartite graph with R >= 4 needs at least 13 vertices. This is a size restriction, not a list of which bipartite graphs have R = 3. It does not bear on non-bipartite graphs.
events.remains: A classification of graphs with R = 3 in general; and within bipartite graphs, which graphs have R = 3 (the paper gives only the upper bound and crown extremality).

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (claimed in the abstract and in Section 1 of the paper, 'verified by its kernel')

events.directly_checkable: Two finite assertions are settled by Boolean unsatisfiability certificates (SAT), per the abstract. The certificate files and their location were not identified. The Lean repository was not located, so whether it still contains sorry was not checked.
events.direction: Upper bound on R for bipartite graphs: R(G) <= ceil(N/4) for N >= 9, with crown graphs attaining it. It does not assert or deny anything about graphs with R = 3 specifically. The bullet's question (classify R = 3) is not addressed.
events.object: No new object is exhibited. The extremal objects are the crown graphs H_{n,n}, with R = ceil(n/2) by Glen, Kitaev and Pyatkin (2016), which the paper cites as the value attaining its bound.

summary: The bullet asks for a classification of all graphs with representation number 3, and no source I opened claims one. The Wikipedia article (fetched via a summarising tool; footer shows last edit 9 August 2026) says 'No classification for graphs with representation number 3 is known' and lists 'Classify graphs with representation number 3' under open problems, and the arXiv and journal pages I read say the same. The window (from 26 January 2024) holds a set of partial results, all restricted to subclasses: exact characterizations of R = 3 within word-representable split graphs and split comparability graphs (Dwary, Mozhui, Krishna, Feb 2025, v2 Apr 2025), within well-partitioned chordal graphs (Dwary and Krishna, Apr 2025, class determined but theorems not read), within co-bipartite graphs (Das and Hariharasubramanian, Sept 2025, v2 June 2026: R = 3 exactly for word-representable non-permutation co-bipartite graphs), and within melon graphs and their line graphs (Mozhui and Krishna, Feb 2026, Theorem 2.3); plus families known to have R = 3 (grid and cylindric grid graphs, Alshammari, Kitaev, Pyatkin, July 2025) and general bounds (R <= 3 for some circulant and square-free-restricted classes; a 2025 bipartite upper bound by Mozhui and Krishna; the Colbrook and Drysdale bipartite bound R <= ceil(N/4) of 24 September 2026). Pre-window background includes Kitaev's 2014 prisms and extensions, Glen-Kitaev-Pyatkin's 2016 crown graph values, and the 2018 computational census. The question is therefore not settled, and the in-window results do not classify R = 3 in general. Close calls: (1) Whether restricted-class classifications should count as progress on the bullet: they fully determine R = 3 inside a subclass but leave the unrestricted question untouched, and the bullet is unrestricted; I record them as partial. (2) Colbrook and Drysdale: the bound is for bipartite graphs and does not classify R = 3, so I record it as not bearing on the classification; but the authors' AI declaration says ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6 contributed to the approach, and ChatGPT 5.6 to the 'classification' used in the proof. That word 'classification' refers to an obstruction classification inside the bipartite proof, not to a classification of R = 3 graphs, which is the source of possible confusion. The AI credit is recorded as load-bearing on the credit's wording, with the judging pass to weigh it. (3) The Colbrook and Drysdale abstract says the main theorem is verified in Lean 4; I did not find the repository and so did not check it for sorry. AI search: about thirty-four web searches looked for AI involvement in the R = 3 literature (names of labs and models, ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini in acknowledgements, Lean formalisations, AI-result trackers). The only AI credit in this area is the Colbrook and Drysdale declaration. The other 2026 AI results I saw (a Cycle Double Cover claim credited to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, the unit-distance counterexample, and a Claude Opus 4.6 Knuth report) are on other problems and are not recorded as events. None of the R = 3 papers I opened (Kitaev 2014, Dwary-Mozhui-Krishna, Das-Hariharasubramanian, Alshammari-Kitaev-Pyatkin, Mozhui-Krishna melon and bipartite) names an AI system. The Wikipedia wording 'Classify graphs with representation number 3' is an open problem with no cited origin that I checked; I did not open the Kitaev-Lozin book (2015, Chapter 7). Pre-window results with classification flavour are the Petersen graph and prism facts, which I took from secondary sources (Konovalov and Linton 2010, not opened) and Kitaev 2014 (opened).
competing_reading: The strongest case for a larger outcome: the in-window work now completely determines R = 3 for several natural subclasses (word-representable co-bipartite graphs, split graphs, split comparability graphs, melon graphs), and together with the bipartite bound these cover a large share of graphs that have R = 3 among small or structured graphs; a reader who counts these as progress would say the problem is 'partly settled by class' and that the record should mark the restricted classifications as events that settle their subclass. The case against: the bullet asks for every graph, and no subclass result touches the non-subclass graphs; the R = 3 members that remain (for example the general prisms and Petersen-type graphs outside these classes) show that the unrestricted class is not described. A second reading of the Colbrook and Drysdale paper: its AI declaration gives ChatGPT credit for 'this approach' and for the 'classification' used in the proof, so a judging pass that treats AI credit as load-bearing for any result in the window would count it; the opposing reading is that its bearing on the bullet is nil, because it is a bipartite upper bound on R and not a classification of R = 3, so it should not be counted as AI-involved progress on this bullet at all.
what_would_settle_it: A published or preprinted description of R = 3 for all graphs (a characterization, forbidden-subgraph list, or theorem stating the class), which I did not find. For the restricted results: the full texts of Dwary-Mozhui-Krishna v2 (to confirm Theorem 3.2 and the family definitions), Dwary-Krishna 2504.04256 (the R = 3 class in well-partitioned chordal graphs), Mozhui-Krishna 2602.14179 (the exact Theorem 2.3 condition against its prose), and the grid paper's journal version (for the cylindric hypothesis). For Colbrook and Drysdale: the Lean repository and its sorry status, the SAT certificates, and any independent reading or erratum; and the authors' fuller account of which parts of the proof came from the ChatGPT discussions. For the open problem itself: the Kitaev-Lozin book (Chapter 7) or the source of the Wikipedia wording, to confirm what 'classify' was meant to ask.

event.what_happened: Tithi Dwary, Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna, 'Representation Number of Word-Representable Split Graphs' (arXiv 2502.00872; v1 2 February 2025, v2 27 April 2025). A split graph has a vertex set partitioned into a clique and an independent set. The authors show that every word-representable split graph has R <= 3, and they characterize the word-representable split graphs with R = 3 (v2 Theorem 3.2: G has R = 3 if and only if G contains an induced graph from the family C3 = F0, the even-k suns (k >= 4), and the odd-k graphs F1(k), F2(k) (k >= 5)). They also characterize split comparability graphs with R = 3 (Theorem 3.4: iff G contains F0 or F1(5) as an induced subgraph). The v2 comment says Fig. 2 was corrected using N. Pardal's PhD thesis, and the proof of Theorem 6 and the subsequent split-comparability results were updated. The family definitions were relayed by a summarising fetch and not read in full.
event.revisions: v1 2 Feb 2025; v2 27 Apr 2025 (Fig. 2 corrected from N. Pardal's thesis; proof of Theorem 6 and split-comparability results updated).
event.delivers: Within the class of word-representable split graphs: R <= 3 always, and R = 3 exactly for graphs containing one of the listed induced families (Theorem 3.2 as relayed by the fetch). Within split comparability graphs: R = 3 exactly when F0 or F1(5) is induced (Theorem 3.4). A characterization of R = 3 restricted to split graphs; it says nothing about graphs that are not split.
event.remains: R = 3 for all word-representable graphs that are not split (in particular all non-split comparability and non-comparability graphs). The authors' conclusion asks next to characterize word-representable split graphs by minimal forbidden induced subgraphs.

What exactly changed in the stated characterization was not compared across versions here.
event.direction: Gives an exact characterization of R = 3 within split graphs and split comparability graphs. It cuts in the direction the bullet expects for those subclasses (R = 3 is determined by explicit forbidden induced families). It is not a classification of R = 3 in general.

events.ai_basis: This approach arose through discussions between the authors and ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6. ... The classification also emerged from discussions between the authors and ChatGPT 5.6.

judgement.why: The statement asks for a classification of all graphs with R = 3, with no restriction to any class. So a complete determination of R = 3 inside one class is a case. That covers split graphs, well-partitioned chordal graphs, co-bipartite graphs, melon graphs, and grids and cylindric grids (every grid with m, n >= 3 has R = 3), and before the snapshot prisms, crowns and book graphs. The census is instances. Reductions, square-freeness results, orientation criteria, upper bounds of the form R <= 3 that do not decide which graphs have R = 3, and prn-only results are none or variant. Upper bounds on R for bipartite graphs answer a different question, the Glen et al. conjecture, and not the R = 3 classification, so Mozhui-Krishna 2025 and Colbrook-Drysdale are variant. Colbrook-Drysdale's AI role is still judged on its own quote: per the authors, ChatGPT supplied the proof's approach and an obstruction classification, so it is assisted. Digested goes only where a journal of record or a thesis committee is on the record. Melon's 'to appear' counts. The grids paper's JALC acceptance rests on an unverified snippet, so it stays unreviewed. No direction is assigned, because a classification question has no conjectured outcome to confirm or refute.
judgement.doubts: Whether the family results (grids, prisms, crowns) should count as case rather than none is a close call. Within their families they determine R exactly, so I treated them as restrictions. Calling the bipartite bounds variant rather than bound means the AI-assisted Colbrook-Drysdale event does not count as movement on this problem. The thesis verification rests on a snippet about the viva-voce.
